name: Raw milk for height

angle.text: Some height-focused communities drink unpasteurised milk in the belief it promotes growth, with proponents citing nutrition and immunity. No height studies of raw milk exist, so the link rests on anecdote.

summary: Drinking unpasteurised milk to grow taller; no height studies exist and the CDC and FDA advise against it.
note: CDC and FDA strongly recommend against raw milk; documented outbreaks.
currentQuick:
Raw milk for height is the belief that unpasteurised milk helps people grow taller. Reference sources show dairy-rich diets track with taller populations but do not single out raw milk.
No study of raw milk and height was found.
How it works: Believers point to the protein and nutrients in milk. Sources report heating does not substantially change nutritional value.
Risks and caveats: The CDC and FDA recommend against raw milk because it can carry pathogens such as Listeria, Salmonella and E. coli, with highest risk in young children, older adults, pregnancy and weakened immunity. Legal status varies by country and US state.
deepLead:
Raw milk for height refers to the belief, circulating in some height-focused online circles under slogans such as Raw Milk + Healthy = Holy Height, that drinking unpasteurised milk promotes growth. Wikipedia defines raw milk as milk that has not been pasteurised and reports that proponents say it tastes better, is more nutritious and supports immunity.
Wikipedia reports that the article finds no clear nutritional or health benefit, that the FDA says pasteurisation does not destroy nutritional value, and that the CDC and FDA strongly recommend against drinking raw milk because of pathogen risk. Wikipedia's article on human height notes that populations eating more dairy and animal protein tend to be taller, without distinguishing raw from pasteurised milk. The sources reviewed do not mention raw milk and height in children.

name: Height-stretching devices / inversion

angle.text: Users hang from inversion tables or gravity boots to decompress the spine and add measurable morning height, with some forum posters reporting about two inches. Reported gains are millimetres and short-lived in the available sources.

summary: Inversion tables and stretch devices for height; any gain reported is millimetres and short-lived.
note: Cardiac, eye-pressure and fall risks are documented for inversion.
currentQuick:
Inversion tables and gravity boots hang a person at an inverted angle to decompress the spine. Forum users discuss them as a way to gain morning height.
Reference sources describe short-term spinal elongation that reverses within about an hour and no strong evidence of lasting height gain in adults.
How it works: Gravity-assisted traction briefly increases spacing between vertebrae, which is the basis of the claimed height effect.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia lists raised heart rate and cardiac workload, acid reflux and ankle discomfort, with higher risk for people with heart disease, hypertension, glaucoma or pregnancy. Grokipedia adds eye pressure and fall injuries.
deepLead:
Height-stretching devices are products marketed or discussed as ways to add height by stretching or decompressing the spine. The best-known examples are inversion tables and gravity boots, which suspend a person at an inverted angle as a form of gravity-assisted spinal traction. In looksmaxxing communities, inversion tables are discussed as a possible way to gain or hold morning height.
Wikipedia reports that gravity-assisted traction briefly increases spacing between vertebrae and that the main reported benefit is a pleasant sensation lasting minutes; its inversion article does not address height. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, reports short-term elongation of roughly 5 to 9 mm after sessions that largely reverses within about an hour, and no strong evidence of lasting multi-centimetre gains in healthy adults. Wikipedia lists cardiac, eye-pressure and reflux concerns for inversion.

name: Posture for height (rib/pelvic tilt)

chain: Correct pelvic tilt and rib flare
angle.text: Forum users correct anterior pelvic tilt and rib flare to stand taller and look more upright, and some ask whether it also improves facial symmetry. Standing straighter changes how tall someone measures and appears; no study measures stature change from these fixes.

summary: Correcting pelvic tilt and rib flare to recover height; forum anecdotes, but no study measures stature change.
note: Pelvic tilt research concerns back pain and spinal deformity, not height.
currentQuick:
Posture for height is the belief that fixing anterior pelvic tilt or rib flare adds centimetres. Forum users report gains of one to two inches after stretching and strengthening.
Clinical literature on pelvic tilt concerns spinal alignment, pain and disability; no study located measured height change.
How it works: Believers say a tilted pelvis exaggerates the lower-back curve and shortens apparent stature, and that stretching hip flexors while strengthening glutes and core restores it.
Risks and caveats: The exercises discussed are ordinary mobility and strength work; sources report no specific harms. Persistent tilt asymmetry can relate to scoliosis or leg-length differences, which Wikipedia says are addressed by clinicians.
deepLead:
Posture for height is the belief in looksmaxxing communities that correcting pelvic tilt, rib flare or related posture patterns can add centimetres to standing height. Forum threads on anterior pelvic tilt (APT) ask whether fixing it would increase height, how to correct it, and whether tilt asymmetry affects facial symmetry.
Pelvic tilt is the orientation of the pelvis relative to the thigh bones and trunk, and Wikipedia describes anterior, posterior and lateral forms with associated muscle patterns and exercise suggestions, noting the article's height link appears only in an image caption and that no effectiveness data are given. Clinical literature on pelvic tilt concerns spinopelvic alignment and its relation to pain and disability in spinal deformity, not height gain in healthy people.

name: Growth-plate peptides (IGF-1/MK-677 for height)

angle.text: Teenagers discuss MK-677 and IGF-1 products as a way to gain height by raising growth hormone signalling. Trials exist in children with growth hormone deficiency; none test healthy short people, so the height use is off-label and rests on anecdote.

summary: Growth hormone secretagogues like MK-677 (and IGF-1 products) pitched as a way to gain height; trials exist only in children with growth hormone deficiency, none in healthy short people.
note: MK-677 is an unapproved investigational drug, and no trials have tested it for height in healthy short individuals.
currentQuick:
This entry covers the practice of using growth hormone (GH) boosting compounds, most often the oral drug MK-677 (ibutamoren) and sometimes IGF-1 products, in an attempt to grow taller before the growth plates close. It sits within the wider height discourse in looksmaxxing communities.
Published research on these compounds is in children and adults with diagnosed growth hormone deficiency or in older adults, not in healthy people who are simply short. Comparisons of GH treatments in deficient children measure height velocity and IGF-1 levels, and a Phase 3 trial of LUM-201 (the pharmaceutical name for ibutamoren) in children with GH deficiency is registered.
How it works: MK-677 mimics ghrelin at the ghrelin receptor and raises GH and IGF-1 levels, which are the hormones that drive growth in childhood. In growth hormone deficiency, injected GH is the standard therapy and is reported to add roughly 5 to 10 cm to predicted adult height in treated short-stature children.
Risks and caveats: MK-677 is an Investigational New Drug and not approved for marketing in the US. Adult studies describe raised cortisol alongside raised GH and IGF-1. No published trial tests these compounds for height in healthy people, and growth plate closure limits any growth window after puberty.
deepLead:
Growth-plate peptides is a looksmaxxing term for the use of growth hormone (GH) secretagogues and related products, chiefly MK-677 (ibutamoren) and IGF-1, with the aim of increasing height. MK-677 is an experimental, orally active drug that stimulates the ghrelin receptor and raises GH and IGF-1 levels.
Research on GH-axis drugs for height concerns children with diagnosed growth hormone deficiency. A 2026 meta-analysis compared once-weekly somatrogon with daily somatropin in prepubertal children with GH deficiency, measuring IGF-1, height SDS and height velocity. A Phase 3 trial of LUM-201, the pharmaceutical name for ibutamoren, in children with GH deficiency is registered. No published trial has tested these compounds for height in healthy short individuals.
Short stature is typically defined medically as adult height more than two standard deviations below the mean, and GH therapy is reported to add about 5 to 10 cm to predicted final height in treated children, at high cost.

name: Manlet / height tiers

angle.text: Manlet and height tiers are community slang for short men and the brackets used to rank them, and they frame why many users pursue height gains, lifts and better presentation. It is a vocabulary of social hierarchy rather than a method with its own evidence.

summary: Community slang for short men and the height brackets used to rank them; mostly a social-hierarchy vocabulary with height a major topic in appearance discourse.
note: Cutoffs vary by poster and are not an established scientific standard; medical short stature is defined statistically.
currentQuick:
Manlet is slang on looksmaxxing forums for a man regarded as short, and height tiers are the informal brackets users employ when ranking men by height. Where the cutoffs fall is itself debated among posters, and no single standard exists.
Threads using the term range from advice requests to memes and screenshots of short and tall people side by side. Height is also the subject of heightmaxxing discussion, including questions about growth hormone drugs and limb surgery.
How it works: There is no mechanism as such. It is a classification vocabulary. Medicine defines short stature as adult height more than two standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, which covers roughly the shortest 2.3 percent of a population.
Risks and caveats: The term is used as a pejorative as well as a self-description in these forums. Medical sources describe teasing reported by short children, and one Swedish cohort study reported an inverse association between height and suicide risk in men, while noting most very short adults are not disabled by their height.
deepLead:
Manlet is slang used on looksmaxxing forums such as looksmax.org for a man considered short, often used with the idea of height tiers: informal brackets of height used to rank men within the community. Posters disagree about where the thresholds sit, and threads exist both asserting and disputing particular cutoffs.
Medically, short stature is usually defined as adult height more than two standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, about the shortest 2.3 percent of a population, and common childhood causes include constitutional growth delay and familial short stature. The community vocabulary is separate from this definition.
Height features heavily in forum discussion, where members post about perceived social disadvantage, rage threads, and 'heightmaxxing' options such as growth hormone secretagogues. The scientific literature on appearance and height cited here is limited.

name: Anabolic steroid stacks (looksmaxxing)

angle.text: Forum users discuss steroid combinations for muscle size and a masculine look, including a wider jaw and neck. Muscle gain from anabolic steroids is well documented; claims about facial bone and skeletal width are untested.

summary: Combinations of anabolic-androgenic steroids and other hormones that forum users discuss for a more muscular, masculine look; documented in medicine mainly for harms and hormonal suppression.
note: Controlled substances in many countries; documented effects include hormonal suppression, cardiovascular and lipid changes, and premature growth plate closure in adolescents.
currentQuick:
A stack is a combination of several anabolic-androgenic steroids, sometimes with growth hormone or other agents, that users take together. On looksmaxxing forums, threads ask for the best stack for muscle, shoulders, a masculine face or a lean look, and some are started by teenagers.
Medical sources describe anabolic steroids as drugs related to testosterone with approved uses such as treating low testosterone and delayed puberty. Their non-medical use for appearance is documented, and most users are described as men around age 25 who use them for how they look.
How it works: Anabolic-androgenic steroids bind and activate the androgen receptor, the same target as testosterone, which drives muscle and secondary sex characteristics. Combinations are chosen by users for different reputed effects, but published studies of specific stacks for facial appearance were not found.
Risks and caveats: Medical sources list unfavourable cholesterol changes, hypertension, heart changes, suppression of the body's own testosterone production, testicular atrophy, fertility impairment, liver damage with some oral forms, acne and hair loss. In adolescents, steroids can prematurely close growth plates and stunt adult height. They are Schedule III in the US and Class C in the UK.
deepLead:
Anabolic steroid stacks are combinations of anabolic-androgenic steroids (AAS), often taken with other hormones, that users on looksmaxxing forums discuss for building muscle and a masculine appearance. Anabolic-androgenic steroids are drugs structurally related to testosterone that act by binding to and activating the androgen receptor.
Medical uses of AAS include testosterone replacement in men with low testosterone, inducing male puberty, treating certain anaemias and wasting conditions, and masculinising hormone therapy. Non-medical use for appearance is documented, with studies describing most users as men with a median age near 25 who use them for how they look.
Documented adverse effects include cardiovascular changes, suppression of natural testosterone production, fertility impairment and, in adolescents, premature closure of growth plates. AAS are controlled substances in the US, UK and Canada.

name: Short steroid cycles myth

angle.text: Users discuss brief steroid courses as a way to gain muscle while limiting lasting effects on the body's hormones. No trial has tested the idea for appearance use, and medical sources describe hormone recovery as variable.

summary: The belief that brief steroid courses avoid the lasting harms of long ones; no trial has tested it for appearance use, and medical sources describe recovery as variable.
note: Only indirect research exists; a harm-reduction trial and a cardiac imaging study in steroid users are registered.
currentQuick:
The claim is that taking anabolic steroids for only a short stretch limits side effects, so that users keep the cosmetic benefit without lasting damage. It circulates in steroid-related discussion online.
Steroid medical literature does say that after short courses, drugs such as clomiphene or hCG can restore normal testosterone production, and that infertility from sperm suppression is usually reversible. These statements are about recovery, not about whether short courses are free of harm, and no published trial compares short and long cycles for safety.
How it works: Anabolic-androgenic steroids suppress the body's own testosterone production through the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. The proposed logic is that a shorter exposure means less suppression and less cumulative organ stress.
Risks and caveats: Medical sources describe cardiovascular, lipid, liver, hormonal and fertility effects and, in adolescents, premature growth plate closure. Whether such effects scale with duration for short courses has not been established by trials found for this entry. Steroids are controlled substances in many countries.
deepLead:
The short steroid cycles claim holds that brief courses of anabolic-androgenic steroids are comparatively safe. It is a belief about how duration relates to risk rather than a defined practice.
Medical sources describe adverse effects of steroids including cardiovascular changes, hormonal suppression and fertility impairment. They note that after short courses, clomiphene or hCG can restore normal testosterone production and that infertility is usually reversible. No trial found compares short and long cycles for safety in appearance-motivated users.

name: TRT / testosterone for jaw

chain: Claimed facial bone and muscle change
angle.text: Users discuss testosterone therapy or related androgens in the hope of a more masculine jaw, midface and neck. Testosterone therapy is established medicine for low testosterone and masculinising treatment; no study tests it for jaw structure in the way looksmaxxers describe.

summary: The idea of using testosterone or related androgens to masculinise the jaw and face; testosterone therapy is established for low testosterone, but no study tests it for jaw structure.
note: Testosterone is a controlled, prescription-only drug in many countries; adverse effects and fertility suppression are documented.
currentQuick:
Some looksmaxxing discussion holds that testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), or related androgens such as DHT, can masculinise the face and jaw. Testosterone medication is approved for men with low natural testosterone, for masculinising therapy in transgender men and for some other uses.
The sources reviewed give no study of testosterone for jaw or facial bone structure in the context of appearance enhancement. Medical descriptions cover hypogonadism, side effects and legal status.
How it works: Testosterone acts on the androgen receptor and is converted in tissues to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by 5-alpha-reductase. DHT is associated with facial and body hair growth and male genital development. Testosterone is linked to musculoskeletal development, voice deepening and libido.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects of testosterone medication include acne, oily skin, hair loss, breast enlargement in men, raised red blood cell count, worsened sleep apnoea, liver toxicity with some forms and suppression of sperm production. Testosterone is Schedule III in the US, Class C in the UK and prescription-only in the EU.
deepLead:
TRT or testosterone for jaw refers to the belief, discussed in looksmaxxing communities, that testosterone replacement or related androgens such as DHT can masculinise the jaw and other facial structure. Testosterone medication is used to treat males with low or absent natural production, for masculinising hormone therapy and for certain breast cancers.
Testosterone is a controlled substance in many places, and it can suppress sperm production, cause acne, hair loss and breast enlargement in men and raise haematocrit. DHT is a testosterone metabolite made by 5-alpha-reductase in target tissues and is linked to facial and body hair growth. No studies were found on testosterone therapy for jaw structure.

name: DHT / Androgel for facial structure

angle.text: Forum users discuss DHT or testosterone gel during puberty to masculinise facial structure and boost beard growth. Gels are studied for low testosterone in older men; their effect on facial bone development is untested and rests on anecdote.

summary: Topical DHT or testosterone gel pitched in forums for masculinising the face during puberty; gels are studied for low testosterone in older men, not for facial structure.
note: Pharmaceutical DHT is not available in the US or Canada; forum use often involves unregulated or homemade products. Trials have been in older men, not adolescents.
currentQuick:
Topical DHT (dihydrotestosterone) gel is promoted by some looksmaxxing posters as a way to enhance brow ridge, jaw and cheek development, especially in puberty. AndroGel is a brand of testosterone gel approved for male hypogonadism, and discussion sometimes uses it alongside or instead of DHT gel.
The human trials found concern older men with low testosterone, looking at well-being, sexual function, cognition and the prostate. None tested facial bone structure or adolescents.
How it works: DHT is made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase and acts locally in tissues. It is linked to facial and body hair, prostate growth and male genital development. Forum proponents argue it drives facial dimorphism, but published studies have not tested that.
Risks and caveats: Testosterone gels can transfer to others by contact and are reported to raise prostate-specific antigen modestly. A trial in healthy men found DHT administration did not raise intraprostatic androgen concentrations. Pharmaceutical DHT is unavailable in the US and Canada.
deepLead:
DHT gel and AndroGel for facial structure is a hormonal protocol discussed on looksmaxxing forums. Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is an androgen made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase in target tissues, and it acts mainly locally. It is associated with facial and body hair, prostate and genital development. AndroGel is a testosterone gel approved for male hypogonadism.
As a medication, DHT is called androstanolone and is sold in forms including topical gels in certain European countries, but it is not available in the US or Canada. Trials of DHT gel have been conducted in older men with symptoms of low testosterone. No study has tested DHT or testosterone gel for facial bone development.

name: Pentastack

angle.text: The pentastack is a mix of Adderall, dextromethorphan, pregabalin, ketamine and BDO that drew attention in 2026 through looksmaxxing influencers, who describe it as a way to feel more composed in public. It is a news event rather than an appearance method, with no studied link to looks.

summary: A five-drug stimulant and depressant mix from 2026 livestream culture; a news event more than a looks method.
note: Combines a stimulant with strong depressants including a GHB precursor; one user was hospitalised after a livestream.
currentQuick:
The pentastack is a mixture of Adderall, dextromethorphan, pregabalin, ketamine and BDO that the Australian influencer Androgenic said he used while livestreaming in 2026.
It is not a method for changing appearance. It became known after the streamer Clavicular was hospitalised on 14 April 2026, an account he disputes.
How it works: There is no appearance mechanism. Users describe it as a way to feel more at ease in public; the components are a stimulant plus sedating and dissociative drugs.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks of the components include seizures, vomiting, additive sedation and a potentially fatal BDO withdrawal. Some components are prescription-only or controlled in many places. No studies of the combination exist.
deepLead:
The pentastack is a term for a five-substance drug combination that came to wider attention in 2026 through looksmaxxing influencers. According to Wikipedia, it consists of Adderall (amphetamine salts), dextromethorphan, pregabalin, ketamine and 1,4-butanediol (BDO), and it combines a stimulant with several central nervous system depressants.
Unlike most entries in looksmaxxing culture, it is not a method for changing physical appearance. It is documented here because it became a widely reported episode in the community, associated with the Australian influencer Androgenic and the streamer Clavicular, who was taken to hospital after a livestream on 14 April 2026.
No clinical studies have examined this specific combination. Its components are individually described in medical literature, and the sources reviewed describe BDO as producing effects similar to its metabolite GHB, with reported risks including seizures, vomiting and a withdrawal syndrome that can potentially be fatal.

name: Weight-loss jabs (GLP-1) for face leaning

angle.text: Users take GLP-1 jabs such as semaglutide to lose weight and, with it, facial fat, aiming for a leaner, more defined face. The facial hollowing sometimes called "Ozempic face" is debated. The medicines are studied for weight loss; their effect on facial appearance specifically is based mostly on anecdote and case discussion.

summary: Appetite-suppressing injectables that lean the face through general fat loss, with 'Ozempic face' hollowing as the debated flip side.
note: Facial effects are a by-product of overall weight loss; compounded and grey-market versions are not FDA-evaluated.
currentQuick:
GLP-1 weight-loss injections such as semaglutide lower appetite and body weight. Some people in looksmaxxing and aesthetic circles use them hoping for a leaner, more defined face.
Trials measured body weight, not faces. Recent reviews discuss "Ozempic face", the hollow or aged look that can follow rapid fat loss.
How it works: The drugs mimic the gut hormone GLP-1, reducing appetite and slowing gastric emptying. Facial change is thought to follow overall loss of body and facial fat.
Risks and caveats: Common effects include nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea; gallstones and a boxed thyroid-tumour warning (from rodent studies) are listed. They are prescription-only, and the FDA says compounded forms have not been shown safe or effective.
deepLead:
Weight-loss jabs are injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist medicines, such as semaglutide (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy), that reduce appetite and body weight. In looksmaxxing and aesthetic-medicine discussion they are sometimes described as a way to lose facial fat and obtain a leaner, more defined face, and the downside of rapid facial fat loss is popularly called "Ozempic face."
Semaglutide was approved in the US for type 2 diabetes in December 2017 and, at a higher dose, for weight management in June 2021. In a phase III trial of 1,961 adults with obesity, mean weight change at 68 weeks was about -14.9% with semaglutide versus -2.4% with placebo. Face leaning is a side effect of general weight loss rather than a targeted effect; no drug in this class is approved for reducing facial fat.
Published clinical literature on the face specifically is mostly recent narrative reviews and surgeon commentaries rather than controlled trials. Several 2026 papers discuss whether "Ozempic face" is a distinct clinical entity and how rapid weight loss affects facial ageing.

name: Peptide stacks (Wolverine stack)

angle.text: Forum users pair BPC-157 with TB-500 (the "Wolverine stack") to speed recovery from injuries and training so they can keep lifting for physique gains. Broader peptide stacks are also discussed for skin, bone mass or height. Support comes from animal data and anecdote, with no human trials on appearance outcomes.

summary: BPC-157 plus TB-500, the recovery-peptide pairing; animal data and forum hope, no human appearance trials.
note: Not approved by any regulator; banned by WADA; human safety data are insufficient.
currentQuick:
The Wolverine stack pairs BPC-157, a gastric-derived peptide, with TB-500, a thymosin beta-4 fragment. Users describe it for injury recovery, and looksmaxxing forums sometimes extend peptide stacks to skin, bone or height.
Evidence is mostly animal research and a few small human studies; none addresses appearance.
How it works: In animal studies BPC-157 shows tissue-protective effects and promotes blood-vessel growth; thymosin beta-4 binds actin and promotes cell migration. Human mechanisms are not established.
Risks and caveats: No regulator has approved BPC-157; health authorities cite insufficient safety data and a theoretical tumour concern. It is WADA-banned. Gray-market products are unregulated.
deepLead:
A peptide stack is a combination of several research or compounded peptides taken together. The "Wolverine stack" is the name commonly given to BPC-157 combined with TB-500, a synthetic fragment related to thymosin beta-4, which proponents associate with tissue repair and recovery. In looksmaxxing forums, "peptide stacks" more broadly can also include growth-hormone secretagogues and copper peptides, discussed for body composition, skin, bone mass or height.
BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid peptide first reported by Predrag Sikirić's group in Zagreb in 1993. Wikipedia describes the human evidence as limited, mostly small studies, and says the peptide is not approved by any drug regulator for human use. Thymosin beta-4 is a 44-amino-acid protein studied in cell and animal work and in phase 2 trials for wound healing and eye conditions; TB-500 is described in doping literature as a synthetic version of an active region.
No clinical study has tested the BPC-157 plus TB-500 combination for appearance outcomes.

name: Anti-estrogen / AI for masculine look

angle.text: Aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole are used off-label to lower oestrogen for a leaner, more masculine look, less water retention and less breast tissue, and by younger users in pursuit of extra height. They are approved for other medical uses; trials in healthy men for these appearance goals are lacking.

summary: Aromatase inhibitors like anastrozole used off-label to cut oestrogen for a leaner look or height; no trials in healthy men.
note: Breast-cancer drugs; documented joint, bone and cardiovascular effects; off-label use for looks or height is untested.
currentQuick:
Aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole block the enzyme that makes oestrogen. Some looksmaxxing and bodybuilding users take them outside medical supervision hoping for a leaner, more masculine look, less breast tissue or extra height.
The drugs are approved for breast cancer and certain paediatric conditions. No trial has tested them for appearance in healthy men.
How it works: They inhibit aromatase, which converts testosterone and other androgens into oestrogens, lowering circulating oestrogen. Oestrogen helps close growth plates, which is the basis of the experimental height idea.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include joint pain, fatigue, hot flushes, bone loss, cardiovascular effects, and rare liver or skin reactions. They are prescription-only and contraindicated in pregnancy; buying them without a prescription is the grey market.
deepLead:
"AI" in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding slang usually means an aromatase inhibitor, a drug such as anastrozole (Arimidex), letrozole or exemestane that blocks the enzyme converting androgens into oestrogens. Users who take these drugs outside a medical indication describe goals such as a leaner, more masculine look, less water retention or breast tissue, controlling oestrogen alongside testosterone use, and, among younger users, taller final height.
Aromatase inhibitors are approved mainly for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women; anastrozole was patented in 1987 and approved for medical use in 1995. Large trials such as ATAC compared anastrozole with tamoxifen in breast cancer. Wikipedia says use in men is off-label, with experimental work in delayed puberty and short stature, and that the drugs are approved for precocious puberty in boys when combined with other medicines.
No published trial has tested aromatase inhibitors for improving the appearance of healthy men. Research on them in men concerns specific medical conditions, and documented adverse effects include joint pain, bone loss and cardiovascular effects.

name: Minoxidil + finasteride stack

angle.text: Known as "fin+min", this pairing is the baseline regimen in looksmaxxing communities for keeping or thickening scalp hair in male pattern hair loss. Both drugs are approved for this use individually and backed by trials; the combination is discussed on forums as the standard starting point.

summary: The standard hair-loss duo of minoxidil and finasteride; both approved and trial-backed, with finasteride's side effects debated.
note: Finasteride carries sexual and mood side-effect warnings; results last only while treatment continues.
currentQuick:
Fin+min combines minoxidil, which stimulates hair growth, with finasteride, which lowers DHT, the hormone behind male pattern hair loss. It is the base regimen most discussed in looksmaxxing hair-retention threads.
Each drug beats placebo in randomised trials and is FDA-approved; trials of the combination itself are small.
How it works: Minoxidil is a vasodilator prodrug that appears to prolong follicle growth; finasteride blocks type II and III 5-alpha-reductase, lowering scalp and serum DHT and slowing follicle miniaturisation.
Risks and caveats: Finasteride is linked to reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, mood effects and, in 2025, EMA-confirmed suicidal thoughts; persistence after stopping is disputed. Minoxidil can cause scalp irritation and, orally, fluid retention and heart effects. Benefits fade when treatment stops.
deepLead:
The minoxidil plus finasteride stack, often abbreviated "fin+min" on forums, is the combined use of minoxidil, which stimulates hair growth, and finasteride, which lowers dihydrotestosterone (DHT), to treat or slow male pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia). Both drugs are FDA-approved for this purpose individually, and the pairing is the baseline hair-loss regimen discussed in looksmaxxing communities.
Finasteride was approved by the FDA at 1 mg for male pattern hair loss in 1997 as Propecia, and topical minoxidil in August 1988 as Rogaine. A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials found treatments including 5% and 2% minoxidil and 1 mg finasteride were superior to placebo for hair outcomes. The drugs act by different mechanisms, and small trials have compared combined topical lotions with minoxidil alone.
Finasteride carries documented sexual, mood and other adverse effects that are contested in their persistence, and in 2025 the European Medicines Agency confirmed suicidal thoughts as a possible side effect.

name: Oral minoxidil

chain: Thicker scalp, brow and beard hair
angle.text: Users take low-dose oral minoxidil as a convenient alternative to topical minoxidil for scalp hair, and also discuss it for eyebrows, beard and lashes. It is used off-label by dermatologists for hair loss, with trials in that area; the facial hair use rests mostly on anecdote and case reports.

summary: Pill minoxidil at low doses for hair loss; trial-backed and widely prescribed off-label, with fluid-retention and heart caveats.
note: Off-label and prescription-only; reported effects include hypertrichosis, fluid retention and rare cardiac events.
currentQuick:
Oral minoxidil is the blood-pressure pill minoxidil used at very low doses, off-label, for hair loss. Dermatologists prescribe it as an alternative to topical minoxidil, and looksmaxxing users also discuss it for brows, beard and lashes.
Reviews and several randomised trials support its use in androgenetic alopecia, though larger dose-comparison studies are still wanted. Results last only while treatment continues.
How it works: It is a prodrug converted in hair follicles to minoxidil sulfate, which opens potassium channels; proposed effects include vasodilation, anti-inflammatory action and growth-pathway signalling.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are excess body hair and fluid retention; others include low blood pressure, rapid heartbeat, headache and, rarely, pericardial effusion. Forum users report bloating. It is prescription-only and not approved for hair loss, and is toxic to pets.
deepLead:
Oral minoxidil is minoxidil taken as a tablet. At high doses it is a prescription blood-pressure drug (Loniten, approved by the FDA in 1979); at much lower doses it is used off-label by dermatologists for hair loss, an approach often called low-dose oral minoxidil (LDOM) that emerged around 2015. It has also become popular in looksmaxxing communities, where users discuss it for scalp hair, eyebrows, beard and lashes.
Reviews report oral minoxidil as effective and generally well tolerated in hair loss, with androgenetic alopecia the most studied condition, but they call for larger randomised trials. A 2024 randomised trial compared daily oral minoxidil with twice-daily topical 5 percent minoxidil in men over 24 weeks, and a 2024 trial of 65 patients compared 1 mg daily oral minoxidil with topical solution. Common effects are excess hair growth (hypertrichosis) and fluid retention, and reviews note dose-dependent cardiovascular effects.
Oral minoxidil is prescription-only and not FDA-approved for hair loss. Forum posts include reports of bloating and discussion of buying tablets without a prescription, which this wiki does not detail.

name: Dutasteride mesotherapy

chain: Hair loss slows, density may improve
angle.text: Clinicians inject dilute dutasteride into the scalp as an off-label hair-loss treatment, discussed in hair communities as an alternative to oral dutasteride or finasteride. Evidence consists of small early trials and a growing set of case reports.

summary: Scalp injections of dutasteride for hair loss: popular off-label, small early trials, and a growing pile of case reports of hair loss at injection sites.
note: Off-label and unapproved; case series describe alopecia at injection sites, and compounded formulations vary between pharmacies.
currentQuick:
Dutasteride mesotherapy means delivering dutasteride, a drug that blocks the conversion of testosterone to DHT, into the scalp through many small intradermal injections instead of swallowing it as a capsule. It is used off-label for androgenetic alopecia (pattern hair loss) and has gained a following among people seeking a way to get the effect locally.
The evidence is early. A network meta-analysis pooled the available trials, a randomized comparison of monthly versus quarterly sessions has been published as a letter, and clinical case series exist. No regulator has approved the technique.
How it works: Dutasteride inhibits type 1 and type 2 (and 3) 5-alpha reductase, lowering DHT, the hormone linked to follicle miniaturization in pattern hair loss. Proponents say that depositing it in the skin keeps systemic absorption negligible while acting on the scalp follicles.
Risks and caveats: Dutasteride is not approved for hair loss in the US, and mesotherapy with it is unapproved. Case series from 2024 to 2026 report non-scarring and persistent alopecia, and anagen effluvium, at injection sites. A 2026 review notes that compounded injectables can contain different excipients, some of which are associated with complement-activation reactions. Oral dutasteride carries a label with sexual and other warnings.
deepLead:
Dutasteride mesotherapy is the off-label practice of injecting dilute dutasteride, a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, into the scalp skin in multiple small intradermal deposits to treat androgenetic alopecia (AGA, or pattern hair loss). It is performed by clinicians, sometimes with a manual needle or a multi-needle device, and is discussed in hair-loss communities as an alternative to oral dutasteride or finasteride. 
Dutasteride itself is approved in the US for benign prostatic hyperplasia and is prescribed off-label for hair loss. It is approved for male pattern hair loss in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan.  The Food and Drug Administration has not approved dutasteride mesotherapy. 
Published evidence is limited. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 33 studies included dutasteride mesotherapy as one of its comparators alongside oral and topical minoxidil, finasteride and dutasteride.  A randomized trial comparing monthly with quarterly sessions was published in 2026 as a letter, and a case series (2024) reported outcomes in treated patients.  Meanwhile, several case series describe hair loss occurring at the injection sites.

name: Jelqing

angle.text: Practitioners use jelqing, a manual stroking technique, in the belief that it enlarges the penis through stretching and tissue remodelling. The idea comes from anecdote and traditional claims; no published clinical studies have measured an enlargement effect.

summary: A manual penis-enlargement technique with no published clinical evidence of effect and clinician warnings about tissue injury.
note: No clinical studies of jelqing were found; clinicians caution against aggressive manipulation.
currentQuick:
Jelqing is a manual technique in which a man strokes or squeezes a semi-erect penis from base toward the head, with the aim of increasing length or girth. It circulates in looksmaxxing forums under labels such as girthmaxxing and lengthmaxxing.
Many people report personal success online, but Wikipedia states that medical evidence is absent. The only peer-reviewed study in this entry's source set concerns men anxious about penis size and notes that they were more likely to attempt methods such as jelqing; it did not test whether jelqing works.
How it works: Proponents describe the mechanism as repeated stretching that causes microscopic tears in erectile tissue which then heal larger. Some forum members counter that stretching enlarges existing erectile chambers without adding new ones, lowering tissue density. Neither account has been tested in clinical studies.
Risks and caveats: Clinicians cited by Wikipedia caution against routine or aggressive jelqing because of possible fibrosis and plaque formation, and the technique may raise the risk of hard flaccid syndrome. Penis size anxiety, which often motivates the practice, has been studied separately as a body dysmorphic concern.
deepLead:
Jelqing is a manual technique that claims to enlarge the penis. Practitioners squeeze and stroke the semi-erect shaft from base toward the head.  The word is said to derive from the Persian phrase jalq zadan, and Wikipedia attributes the technique to ancient Arab origins. 
Many people describe personal gains in online communities, but Wikipedia states that medical evidence for the technique is absent and that journalists have called it biologically implausible.  Clinicians quoted there generally advise against routine jelqing and caution that aggressive manipulation may cause fibrosis and plaque formation or contribute to hard flaccid syndrome. 
In looksmaxxing communities, jelqing is discussed alongside other physical enlargement methods such as vacuum pumps and stretching devices, under terms such as girthmaxxing and lengthmaxxing.

name: Hair oiling

angle.text: A long-standing South Asian practice, hair oiling uses coconut oil or herbal blends on hair and scalp for shine, softness and scalp care. In looksmaxxing circles it is also discussed for growth and slowing graying. Lab data and surveys exist; trials for growth or graying are lacking.

summary: Applying oil to hair and scalp, a long-standing South Asian practice; lab data and surveys exist, but growth or anti-graying claims lack trials.
note: Evidence is limited to lab fiber tests, a case-control study and self-reported surveys; scalp irritation and dandruff are reported by some users.
currentQuick:
Hair oiling is the practice of applying oils such as coconut oil to the hair and scalp, often with a massage and often left on for some hours. It is deeply rooted in Indian culture and has been spread further by social media.
The research is thin. A laboratory study found that coconut oil, but not mineral oil, changed the mechanical properties of hair fibers after repeated washes. A case-control study found that oiling appeared protective against premature graying, and a large Indian survey recorded dandruff, itch and hair fall among participants.
How it works: Proponents say oils condition the hair and nourish the scalp. In lab tests of single hair fibers, penetration of coconut oil was reported to make the fiber core more flexible, helping it cope with twisting stress. No trial has shown that oiling increases hair growth.
Risks and caveats: In a 2026 survey of 1,200 people in southern India, 25 percent reported dandruff, 15 percent an itchy scalp and 10 percent hair fall, and many with scalp problems said they would consider changing their routine on dermatologist advice. The survey is self-reported and cannot show cause.
deepLead:
Hair oiling is the application of oils, often coconut oil or herbal blends, to the hair and scalp, usually with a massage. It is a traditional practice in India, where a head massage called champi is common and often uses oil or herbal preparations. 
Research is limited. Laboratory work has tested how oils affect hair fibers, a case-control study found an association between hair oiling and lower odds of premature graying, and a large survey in southern India described the prevalence of dandruff, itch and hair fall among people who oil.  The practice has also become a topic of debate among dermatologists, who weigh possible benefits and risks.

name: NoFap / semen retention

angle.text: Followers of NoFap and semen retention abstain in the belief that it raises testosterone, confidence and attractiveness. The testosterone claim traces to a 2003 study that was later retracted; the looks and confidence benefits themselves have not been shown in studies.

summary: Abstaining from masturbation or ejaculation for supposed looks, testosterone and confidence gains; the claimed benefits have not been shown in studies.
note: Medical authors describe the claimed benefits as unsubstantiated; researchers have documented distress linked to abstinence framing and a Dhat-like anxiety syndrome.
currentQuick:
NoFap and semen retention are two overlapping practices of deliberately avoiding masturbation or ejaculation. NoFap began in 2011 as an online self-help community aimed at quitting pornography and masturbation. In looksmaxxing circles, abstinence is promoted as a route to more confidence, energy and an improved appearance.
Published reviews describe the claimed benefits as unsubstantiated, and a 2024 survey of online ejaculation-training courses found no instructors with medical or mental-health credentials. A widely cited 2003 study on testosterone rising after seven days of abstinence was retracted in 2021.
How it works: Proponents propose that retaining semen conserves nutrients or hormones, raises testosterone, or restores dopamine sensitivity, and so improves mood, skin, jawline or attractiveness. No published study has demonstrated these effects for looks.
Risks and caveats: Researchers have analyzed distress tied to abstinence and relapse framing in NoFap communities, and a 2024 letter describes a Dhat-like syndrome in anti-masturbation groups. The practice itself involves no substance, but men's-health content on social media has been rated as largely inaccurate.
deepLead:
NoFap is an online movement and community whose members try to stop pornography use and masturbation, and semen retention is the related practice of deliberately reducing or stopping ejaculation.  Wikipedia says NoFap was founded in June 2011 by Alexander Rhodes after a Reddit thread about a 2003 study claiming testosterone rose after seven days of abstinence, a study that was retracted in 2021. 
Members cite religious or moral reasons, self-improvement, and physical benefits such as energy, focus and sleep.  In looksmaxxing communities the practice is also discussed as a way to improve confidence, social behavior or appearance. 
Medical authors describe the claimed benefits as lacking evidence. A 2024 study of online ejaculation-training programs found courses promoted with unsubstantiated health claims, and an analysis of TikTok and Instagram found semen retention had the most impressions of the men's-health topics studied, with accuracy rated poor overall.  Pornography addiction and sex addiction are not recognized as diagnoses in the DSM-5-TR or ICD-11, according to Wikipedia.

name: Carnivore diet

angle.text: People eating only animal foods describe clearer skin, a leaner body and a more defined jaw as benefits. Some also credit it with higher testosterone and strength. Human evidence for these appearance outcomes is sparse and rests mainly on testimonials.

summary: An animal-foods-only diet promoted online for skin, leanness and jaw definition; human evidence is sparse and mainly raises nutrient and cholesterol questions.
note: A 2026 scoping review found nine human studies of very limited quality, with reported nutrient shortfalls and raised LDL cholesterol.
currentQuick:
The carnivore diet restricts food to animal products such as meat, eggs and dairy, excluding fruit, vegetables and grains. Its modern popularity dates from around 2018, and it appears in looksmaxxing communities as a way to get leaner, clearer skin or a better jaw and body composition.
Human evidence is thin. A 2026 scoping review located nine human studies and described the quality of evidence as very limited because of small samples, short durations and a lack of controls. Studies of appearance outcomes such as skin or facial structure were not found.
How it works: Proponents say eliminating plant foods removes irritants and processed foods and increases protein and fat intake, which they link to leanness, hormone levels or skin. Reviewers describe the diet as a form of ketogenic eating with unclear long-term effects on nutrients and metabolism.
Risks and caveats: Reviews report potential shortfalls of vitamins C and D, calcium, magnesium, iodine and fiber, and higher LDL and total cholesterol. Wikipedia reports that dietetic bodies, including the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia, reject the diet, and that high red meat intake is linked to higher risks of colon cancer and gout.
deepLead:
The carnivore diet is an almost exclusively animal-based dietary pattern, permitting meat, eggs and dairy and eliminating plant foods.  Wikipedia notes antecedents in nineteenth-century meat-and-water regimens and dates modern promotion to around 2018, when surgeon-turned-advocate Shawn Baker published a book on it; a stricter beef, salt and water version called the lion diet later spread on TikTok. 
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a route to skin, leanness, body composition and jaw or bone-related claims, with other members arguing against it. 
A 2026 scoping review identified nine human studies, noting reported weight loss, increased satiety and improvements in some inflammatory or metabolic markers, alongside risks of nutrient deficiencies and elevated cholesterol, with evidence quality described as very limited.  Wikipedia reports that nutrition scientists and dietetic bodies generally reject it.
